method: WebSearch retrieval. Reddit-targeted queries returned no indexed links; community pain evidenced via first-person Medium essays, ADHD coaching blogs, ADDitude/ADDA, forum threads. Quotes labeled verbatim-from-search-result vs paraphrase.
angle_summary: A compounding pipeline failure around one's own thoughts: weak working memory means ideas evaporate seconds after arising; racing thoughts peak at night when capture is hardest; capture tools that demand a filing decision (Notion, Obsidian) trigger decision paralysis and silent abandonment; and what does get captured scatters into a 'notes graveyard' that is never reviewed and can't be searched. A wave of new 'brain dump' startups confirms both the pain and that mainstream note apps fail ADHD users.

problems.name: Thoughts evaporate before they can be captured
problems.description: Working-memory deficits mean ideas, insights, and intentions vanish seconds after arising — mid-sentence, mid-task, in the shower, or while driving — before any app can even be opened. The loss is emotionally painful, not just inconvenient.
problems.frequency_signal: Described as a 'hallmark symptom of ADHD'; an entire product category (voice-first capture apps) now exists to address it.

evidence.text: Especially if the lost thought felt important—like a spark of insight, a plan, a curiosity, or something you really meant to act on—when it vanishes, it's like being betrayed by your own mind.
evidence.source: InFocus First, 'ADHD Forgetfulness: Why It Happens'

evidence.text: Even if we lived in total isolation, we'd still generate the same ideas over and over again, wishing we could remember them at the right time.
evidence.source: ADDitude Magazine, 'Too Many Ideas in My ADHD Brain'

evidence.text: Working memory challenges look like doing one or two steps of a task, getting distracted, and saying 'Wait, what was I just doing?' — even a brief sneeze is enough to lose track of a thought.
evidence.source: ADHD Solutions LLC / Mental Health Forum thread

evidence.text: First-person essay title: 'Dear ADHD Brain, The Tragic Fate of My Brilliant Ideas'; coaches recommend dry-erase markers on the bathroom mirror and notepads in every room because ideas won't survive the walk to a device.
evidence.source: Elizabeth Lord, MA, CPC on Medium; adhdhomestead.net/write-on-the-wall/

problems.existing_solutions: Notepads in every room, shower markers, voice memos, phone Notes; new AI voice-capture apps (Audionotes, Braindump, Brain Spill).
problems.gap: Analog workarounds fragment capture across dozens of surfaces; phone capture's unlock-open-app-type sequence outlasts the thought. Capture must be near-zero-latency and flow into one findable place.

problems.name: Racing thoughts at night with no good capture outlet
problems.description: ADHD brains race hardest at bedtime — looping on ideas and undone tasks 'because it's afraid of forgetting.' The moment of highest thought volume is when opening a phone is most self-destructive, so thoughts are either lost or cost hours of sleep.
problems.frequency_signal: Up to 70% of people with ADHD report insomnia; multiple ADDitude articles, ADDA Q&As, clinics, and Etsy printables target this exact moment.

evidence.text: Up to 70% of people with ADHD report insomnia, most often difficulty falling asleep.
Your brain races because it's afraid of forgetting; dumping everything gives it permission to shut down.
evidence.source: Built for ADHD, 'The ADHD Brain Dump Method'

evidence.text: Research found racing thoughts in adults with ADHD increased in the evening and at bedtime and tracked with insomnia severity; ADDA advises paper and pen on the nightstand; advice explicitly warns the bedtime brain dump should be analog because 'the phone hands you a hundred new loops the moment you unlock it.'

problems.existing_solutions: Paper notebook on nightstand, pre-bed brain-dump rituals and printable templates, white noise, sleep-hygiene formulas.
problems.gap: Paper capture at 2am produces illegible, unsearchable scraps disconnected from the digital system; phone capture destroys sleep. No mainstream app has a night-safe, frictionless capture mode that routes nighttime thoughts back into next-day workflow.

problems.name: Filing decisions kill capture: Notion/Obsidian-style tools demand executive function ADHD doesn't have
problems.description: Every save forces a taxonomy decision ('Which folder? What tags?'), turning a 2-second capture into decision paralysis. Setup and maintenance overhead leads to enthusiastic builds followed by silent abandonment.
problems.frequency_signal: Dedicated explainer articles ('Why Your ADHD Brain Hates Notion'); community consensus that Obsidian requires a stripped-down setup; abandonment described as 'common and expected.'

evidence.text: Notion requires an organizational decision at the moment of every save and ongoing maintenance afterward, and ADHD specifically makes in-the-moment decision-making and consistent maintenance unreliable, so the system gets silently abandoned despite an enthusiastic setup. It's a design-fit problem, not a willpower problem.
Because ADHD brains struggle with consistency, you end up with 47 tags that mean roughly the same thing and zero confidence you'll ever find anything again.

Most productivity apps assume you will remember the task long enough to open the app, find the right list, type the task, assign a priority, and set a due date. For someone with ADHD, that sequence is often three steps too many.
evidence.source: Recallify, 'ADHD Productivity Tools: What Actually Works (2026 Guide)'

evidence.text: ADHD users report Obsidian's learning curve, plugins, backlinks and graph features create decision paralysis and a temptation to endlessly build the 'perfect' system instead of taking notes.
evidence.source: ADHD/Obsidian community discussion; Shuvangkar Das blog

problems.existing_solutions: Minimalist Obsidian vaults, pre-made templates, 'capture first, organize later' advice, Apple Notes.
problems.gap: Organization is offloaded onto the user in every mainstream tool. ADHD users need zero-decision capture with organization done FOR them (auto-categorization, auto-linking) — currently offered mostly by tiny new startups, not incumbents.

problems.name: The notes graveyard: captured but never findable or revisited
problems.description: Even when capture succeeds, notes scatter across Apple Notes, notebooks, sticky notes, Word docs, and paper scraps. Retrieval fails, and writing something down licenses the brain to forget it — notes are written once and never reviewed.
problems.frequency_signal: Called 'often the top problem for people with ADHD'; a Medium author described decluttering 4,000 accumulated Apple Notes.

evidence.text: I know I wrote it down somewhere… But is it in my Apple Notes, my Kindle highlights, Scrivener, a random Word document, one of my notebooks, or on one of the pieces of paper that's floating around my house?
clutter that stared back at me, silently mocking my disorganization
evidence.source: Mohamed Dosou on Medium — 'How I Decluttered 4,000 Apple Notes' ('hundreds of untitled notes', 'forgotten ideas')

evidence.text: scattered sticky notes, digital files lost in a maze of folders, half-remembered flashes of genius drifting into the ether
evidence.source: Theo James on Medium, 'Note-Taking for ADHD'

evidence.text: Finding notes taken long ago is described as the top problem for people with ADHD — they won't know which of hundreds of places holds the note; many ADHD brains 'seem to think that once something has been written down, they can then forget about it' — so notes are never reviewed.

problems.existing_solutions: Advice to centralize into one system, scheduled review rituals, search/tagging, professional organizers.
problems.gap: All existing fixes require the exact habit-consistency ADHD lacks. Nothing proactively resurfaces old notes at the moment they're relevant; search only works if you remember what you wrote and where.

problems.name: Chronic app-hopping and system abandonment (the productivity 'ADHD tax')
problems.description: Novelty-seeking dopamine makes every new note app feel like 'maybe this will finally work'; users cycle through dozens of tools, leaving data stranded in each. Once an app isn't visually present, it ceases to exist.
problems.frequency_signal: A Medium author documented deleting 47 productivity apps; abandonment called 'common and expected with ADHD'; a whole genre of 'why apps fail ADHD brains' content.

evidence.text: Out of sight, out of mind isn't just a saying for us — it's a neurological reality.
evidence.source: Raymond Brunell on Medium, 'I Deleted 47 Productivity Apps in 30 Days'

evidence.text: ADHD brains crave novelty, as a shiny new planner or app brings a dopamine rush, that exciting feeling of "maybe this will finally work."

App abandonment is 'almost always a design mismatch, not a personal failure'; the ADHD tax includes paying for forgotten subscriptions; first-person accounts include 'Every Productivity App Failed My ADHD Brain. So I Built My Own.'

problems.existing_solutions: Commitment devices, subscription-audit apps, ADHD-specific apps marketing 'the last app you'll switch to.'
problems.gap: Each switch orphans past notes. A sticky solution needs ambient visibility/resurfacing and near-zero maintenance so there is nothing to abandon — plus painless import of the wreckage from prior apps.
